articles.title: Audio Deadlines: Running On-Device TTS Without Audible Glitches
articles.excerpt: Gradium open-sourced Phonon, its on-device TTS engine (https://gradium.ai/phonon). That matters less because of the model than because of what it signals: on-device speech synthesis is now a dependenc…
articles.body: Gradium open-sourced Phonon, its on-device TTS engine ( https://gradium.ai/phonon ). That matters less because of the model than because of what it signals: on-device speech synthesis is now a dependency you can ship rather than a research demo. And a wave of teams is about to find out that the hard part of edge speech is not the model. It is that audio is the one component in your app with a hard real-time deadline, and nothing else in your background trained you for that. Two clocks, and only one of them forgives you A web request can take 900 ms and nobody dies. An audio callback cannot take 21 ms when it had 20. Once playback starts, the DAC consumes samples at a fixed rate forever, and your synthesis loop has to stay ahead of it.

articles.title: I stopped reviewing my coding agent's diffs file by file
articles.excerpt: When I wrote code by hand, a change took me hours. By the time it was done, I knew it by heart: what called what, which path a request took, which test covered which piece. I had built that picture wh…
articles.body: When I wrote code by hand, a change took me hours. By the time it was done, I knew it by heart: what called what, which path a request took, which test covered which piece. I had built that picture while typing, so reviewing it was easy. My coworkers' code was easy to keep up with too. They moved at the same pace I did, so pull requests came in slowly enough that I had time to understand each one. Now a coding agent writes most of the code. A change that took an afternoon lands in minutes, then the next one, then the next. The code changes so often that I no longer build a mental map of it the way I used to. So reviewing became the hard part.

articles.title: Our webhook dedupe check was a race, not a guard
articles.excerpt: We deduplicated webhooks the obvious way. Handler receives an event, runs SELECT on processed_events by event_id, and if nothing is found, does the work and inserts the row at the end. It held for mon…
articles.body: We deduplicated webhooks the obvious way. Handler receives an event, runs SELECT on processed_events by event_id, and if nothing is found, does the work and inserts the row at the end. It held for months. Then a customer got two receipt emails and a loyalty-points credit twice for the same payment. The cause: the gateway redelivered the event 40 ms after the first attempt, because our first response was slow (a cold DB connection pushed it to about 3 seconds, and their timeout was 2). Both deliveries landed on different pods. Both ran the SELECT before either had inserted. Both saw an empty table, and both did the work. In logs it looked like duplicate delivery, but the gateway was behaving correctly. Our check-then-act was the bug. The fix was to flip the order.

articles.title: When both needs are valid: negotiating conditions for working together
articles.excerpt: Social capabilities across human development | Part 13 One person wants quiet; another thinks by talking. Neither is necessarily wrong. Negotiation's social role extends beyond persuading someone to a…
articles.body: Social capabilities across human development | Part 13 One person wants quiet; another thinks by talking. Neither is necessarily wrong. Negotiation's social role extends beyond persuading someone to adapt: it creates conditions in which people with different purposes can act together. Different working styles in the same room Two students prepare a joint presentation. One needs to read silently; the other wants to develop ideas aloud at a whiteboard. They agree on quiet reading first and discussion afterwards. Ideas to discuss can be noted while waiting. This fictional example adjusts time, place, and sequence rather than attempting to fix someone's personality. Consider whether only one person repeatedly yields, alongside whether agreement is reached.

articles.body: Originally published on hexisteme notes . While evaluating Qwen3-TTS for narration, I ran a small A/B to see whether an instruction could raise the speaking rate. It couldn't, I wrote that down, and speed control moved to post-processing. The next day a different experiment turned up a line of code that made half of that A/B meaningless: on the smaller model, the instruction never reached the model. The call returned normal audio, the transcript was perfect, and nothing in the measurements looked wrong. Before comparing settings of a control knob, show that the knob moves the output at all. Otherwise the comparison measures nothing. The A/B The goal was fast narration, around 230 words per minute.

articles.body: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.  Launching in 2027, Artemis III will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano aboard the Orion spacecraft into low Earth orbit to perform a series of demonstrations with test versions, or test articles, of human landing systems being developed by industry partners Blue Origin and SpaceX. During the planned 14-day mission, crews and flight controllers will practice the rendezvous, docking, habitation, and operational procedures that will be essential when Artemis astronauts begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole in 2028.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
articles.excerpt: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station . The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts. Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station , they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node. After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module.
